content.text:
I've read the calendar's topbar, the board's drag code, the data layer and the local file mirror. Here's what the code already settles, so I won't ask about it:

- **Every file is already on the device.** The repo is mirrored into IndexedDB (`shared/store.js`, `allFiles(prefix)`), so search can run locally and offline, results can update on every keystroke, and nothing has to go to the GitHub API.
- **The magnifier is the zoom button today** (`calendar/ui.js:145`). Giving it to search means zoom needs a new icon, as you said.
- **Board drag is desktop-only by design** (`kanban.js:54`, it sets `draggable` only when not on a phone). Phones get ‹ › arrows on each card. HTML5 drag-and-drop doesn't fire on touch, so mobile drag means rewriting it with pointer events.
- **Moving one occurrence of a repeating entry already works**: `patchOccurrence` writes an override, which is what the board does now.
- **Calendar is the only app.** `spike/` is a test page.

**Question 1: what does "installed globally" mean for search?**

Since calendar is the only app, "global" can mean two things:

- **(A) A shared module.** Add `shared/search.js` for the search box, the live results and markdown-aware matching. Each app calls it with its own folder (`calendar/`) and a function that turns a result into a row it can open (for calendar, opening the entry popup). The main Mine screen gets no search.
- **(B) Option A, plus a search on the Mine home screen** that covers all of mine-data and hands each result to the app that owns it.

**I recommend A.** It matches "for the calendar app it shall only search the calendar folder", and with one app the home-screen search in B would only repeat the calendar's own. B can be added later without changing A.

Which one do you mean, or something else?
A

**Question 2: what should "markdown-optimized" mean in practice?**

My proposal for matching:

- **Fields searched:** the frontmatter `title` counts most, then the body. For calendar, also the group's label and the participants. Other frontmatter keys are left out, so `stage: todo` doesn't turn up for "todo".
- **Body read as text, not syntax:** `**bold**`, `# headings`, `- [ ]` checkboxes and backticks are stripped before matching, and a link matches on its visible text, not its URL.
- **Query:** every word has to appear somewhere (AND), each word can match the start of a word (`dent` finds "dentist"), and case and accents are ignored (`cafe` finds "Café"). No fuzzy or typo matching.
- **Ranking:** title matches come first, then body-only matches. Within each group, the closest date to today goes first, upcoming before past.
- **Results:** one row per file, with the title, the date and a short snippet of the body around the match with the matched words highlighted.

Does this match what you meant, or did you have something else in mind, such as full fuzzy search or searching any frontmatter key?

Sounds good. Keep in mind: The search shall be generic. New app might not have the same frontmatter or not frontmatter at all (e.g. zettels in a Zettelkasten). This search shall work for all tools. We can add global requirement that all markdown have at least a title and date though.

Understood. The shared module then can't know anything about calendar fields, so I'm changing two things:

- **No calendar-only fields.** Group label and participants are out. Search covers the title and the body. Other frontmatter values I'd also search, but with body weight. The cost is that `todo` finds tasks in that stage, which is harmless since that text really is in the file.
- **The module only sees files, not entries.** It returns a path, title, date and snippet. The app decides what clicking a result does: calendar opens the entry popup, and a Zettelkasten would open the zettel.

**Question 3: where do the title and date come from? Is that a requirement or a fallback?**

Calendar files already have `title:` but store their date as `start:`, not `date:`. A hard rule of "frontmatter must have `title` and `date`" would mean renaming `start` in every calendar file or making an exception for it. It would also make a hand-written zettel with no frontmatter impossible to find.

I recommend a **fallback chain in the search** plus a **soft rule in the root REQUIREMENTS.md**:

- **title:** frontmatter `title`, else the first `# heading`, else the file name.
- **date:** frontmatter `date`, else `start`, else a `YYYY-MM-DD` in the path, else none. A file with no date ranks after the dated ones and shows no date.
- **The rule:** "Every markdown file should have a title and a date. Search reads them from `title` and `date`/`start`, falling back to the first heading and the path." This states the convention without making a file that breaks it disappear.

Shall I go with this, or do you want a strict requirement so the search can skip the fallbacks?

when the apps call the search they could provide their frontmatter fields. The search would have to take these as parameters. This way we have a generic search while still being able to support specific apps like calendar

Good idea. Each app says which keys mean what, and the module stays generic. My proposal for the call:

```js
openSearch({
  folder: 'calendar/',
  title:  'title',                  // key holding the title
  date:   'start',                  // key holding the date
  fields: ['group', 'participants'],// extra keys searched, at body weight
  open:   path => …                 // what clicking a result does
})
```

- **Keys left out fall back** to the first `# heading` / file name for the title and a date in the path for the date. A Zettelkasten can call it with just `{ folder, open }`.
- **Only keys the app lists are searched**, which drops my earlier "every frontmatter value" idea. `stage: todo` no longer matches unless the app asks for it.

**Question 4: which files in the folder count as documents?**

`calendar/` also holds `groups.md`, `settings.md` and override files. An override holds only the keys that differ, usually with no `title`. None of these should be results of their own.

I recommend this rule: **if the app names a `title` key, a file without it isn't a document.** That drops groups, settings and title-less overrides with no special cases. A repeating entry then shows up once, as its series file, and calendar's `open` opens its next occurrence from today, or the last one if the series has ended. The catch is that an override that rewrote one occurrence's body won't be found by words that appear only in that body. I think that's acceptable.

Would you rather have an explicit `skip` list or predicate instead, or does the title-key rule work?
title key rule sounds good

**Question 5: how the search popup behaves.**

My proposal:

- **Placement:** a centred popup like the day preview. The top row is the text input with the cursor already in it (the phone keyboard opens straight away) and the `x` rightmost. Results are listed below and scroll.
- **Live:** the list updates on every keystroke. With a few thousand small files in memory that's fast, so there's no debounce. The list is capped at 50 rows, with a "50+ matches, keep typing" line when there are more.
- **Empty input:** the list is empty.
- **Clicking a result** opens the entry popup over the search. Closing the entry brings you back to the search with the query and scroll position kept, so you can try the next result. The `x` or Escape on the search closes it.
- **Filter:** search ignores the calendar filter. When you're looking for something, a hidden group quietly dropping results would be confusing. The module stays simpler too, with no filter hook.

**Question 6: topbar layout and the zoom icon.**

Today the bar is `[board][zoom] ‹ period › [menu][home]`. On a phone the two sides form row 1 and `‹ period ›` is row 2. Search and filter add two buttons.

**Layout, three buttons a side so the phone's first row stays balanced:**
```
[board][zoom][search]   ‹ period ›   [filter][menu][home]
```
The filter's active-count badge moves from the hamburger to the filter button. The hamburger keeps just **settings** and **logs**, still as a two-row menu rather than a direct link, since two errands still need naming.

**Zoom icon.** The magnifier goes to search, and the board button already shows three columns. I recommend **the button shows its current state as text instead of an icon**: `D`, `W`, `M` or `Y` in a calendar view (rendered like the `24h` and `!` glyphs). On the board it shows a small icon of the current orientation: three bars side by side for horizontal, three stacked for vertical. That tells you where you are as well as where to tap, which no generic "view" icon does.

The alternative is a fixed **layers** icon (two stacked diamonds), the usual "change view" symbol, which looks the same in every mode.

Do you want the state-showing button or a fixed icon? And does the 3 + 3 layout work for you?

**Question 7: dragging the topbar to the top or bottom.**

The bar is almost all buttons, so a plain drag would fight with taps. Some decisions:

- **How it's grabbed:** press and hold anywhere on the bar for about 400 ms, buttons included. The bar lifts, follows your finger or mouse, and on release snaps to whichever half of the screen it's in. A tap or a short press stays a tap. The other option is a small grip handle, but there's no free room for one on the phone's first row.
- **Scope:** one position for the whole calendar app, month and board alike, remembered per device the way the board orientation is (`setKV`).
- **What follows it:** when the bar is at the bottom, the sync line moves to the top so they don't stack. The popups anchored to bar buttons (zoom, picker, filter, menu) open upward. On a phone at the bottom the rows swap order, so `‹ period ›` sits on the upper row and the icons are nearest the thumb. The bar also respects the home-indicator safe area.

**A simpler option:** a "toolbar: top / bottom" row in settings would do the same thing with none of the gesture code. Since you asked for drag-and-drop I'd build the press-and-hold drag, but say if a settings row is good enough.

Should I go with press-and-hold drag, the settings row, or both?
sounds good. do drag n drop

**Question 8: dragging cards on the phone board.**

Horizontal on a phone shows one column at a time, so the drop target is usually off screen. My proposal:

- **One drag implementation for every device.** Pointer events replace the current HTML5 drag on desktop too, because HTML5 drag doesn't fire on touch. The same small helper drives the board, the calendar grids and the topbar.
- **Pick up with press-and-hold (~400 ms)**, like the topbar, so a normal swipe still scrolls the column. The card lifts and follows your finger. On a desktop with a mouse, pick-up happens after a few pixels of movement with no hold.
- **While a card is held on the phone's horizontal board, three drop zones appear** in a strip over the column header, `todo · doing · done` in their stage colours. You drop on one. That's a better fit than pushing against the screen edge to page the columns, which is fiddly and easy to trigger by accident. Stacked (vertical) needs no strip: you drop on the stage itself, and the board scrolls when you hold near the top or bottom edge.
- **The ‹ › arrows on phone cards are removed.** They exist only because there was nothing to drag onto (`kanban.js:105`), and keeping them means two ways to do one thing, right next to the header's look-alike pager. Tapping a card still opens it, and the popup can still change the stage.

**Question 9: dragging entries between dates.**

- **Views:** month and week. The day view has only one day to drop on, and the year view draws coloured days rather than entries, so neither gets drag.
- **Pick-up:** the same press-and-hold as the board. On a phone a short press still opens the entry and a swipe still scrolls.
- **Target is a day.** In the week view the entry keeps its time even if you drop it at another height in the hour grid; only the column (the day) counts, as you said. Timed entries keep their wall-clock time in the configured zone, so a 09:00 stays 09:00 across a DST change.
- **Multi-day:** whichever day of the span you grabbed, the day you release on becomes the new start, and the end moves by the same number of days.
- **Repeating entries:** dragging moves that one occurrence only, as an override, the same way the board moves one. There's no "move the whole series" option.
- **Tasks** move with their dates. If that moves one into another sprint, it changes boards, which is how sprints already work.
- **Only drawn lines can be dragged.** Entries hidden behind a month cell's `+3` can't, and neither can entries in the day preview.

## Markdown bodies

Every app keeps its text as markdown, so every app has to show it. **One renderer, in `shared/`,
used by all of them** — the calendar's details body today, a zettelkasten note and a diary entry
next. Two renderers would drift, and a note that looked right in one app and wrong in the next
would be the plainest possible sign that these files are not as portable as the whole idea claims.

It is **deliberately small**, and covers what a personal note actually holds: paragraphs, `#` to
`###` headings, bullet and numbered lists, `- [ ]` and `- [x]` checkboxes, **bold**, *italic*,
`code`, and links. No tables, no blockquotes, no fenced code blocks and no images — each of them
is more code to own for something an agenda or a diary page rarely carries, and the app that first
genuinely needs one can add it then.

A checkbox is **rendered, not operated**: `- [x]` draws a ticked box, and ticking it is an edit of
the text like any other. A body is read far more often than its checklist is advanced, and a
tappable box would have to write a file from a screen whose whole point is that it writes nothing.

**It builds nodes, never HTML.** The renderer makes DOM elements and sets text, so nothing in a
body can turn into markup: a body carrying a `<script>` tag shows that tag as text. This is the
threat the CSP exists for — injected script on our own origin — and a data file in your own repo
is the likeliest thing to carry a stray angle bracket. A link is rendered only for `http`, `https`
and `mailto`; anything else stays text, so a `javascript:` URL is never something to press. Links
